content: The implementation of interventions and services for HIV prevention, testing, and treatment involves significant impacts and costs. Directly counting the number of people living with HIV, those newly infected, or those who have died from HIV-related causes is not feasible. Therefore, modeled estimates are used to provide insights into these figures. These models integrate data from geographical and population-specific surveys, as well as other surveillance data sources such as case reporting, mortality statistics, programmatic data, and clinical data. They also incorporate assumptions about HIV transmission and survival to estimate outcomes. Modeled estimates, along with their confidence intervals, offer a scientifically valid method to describe the levels and trends of the HIV epidemic. Tools like the UNAIDS-supported Spectrum AIM model can identify areas with the highest transmission risks and guide countries in addressing programmatic gaps. These tools can also generate ageand gender-specific estimates of people living with HIV and new infections at subnational levels. Using software like Spectrum allows for comparisons of estimates over time and across countries, which is essential for tracking progress toward the Sustainable Development Goals. These models are regularly updated and refined to reflect the latest understanding of the HIV epidemic. Modeling tools can also address other programmatic questions. For instance, the Spectrum Goals module can explore the number of adult HIV infections averted by antiretroviral therapy (ART) or prevention interventions under different criteria and scale-up rates. Resource needs modules can estimate the impact of new recommendations on AIDS-related mortality, infant infections, treatment needs, and associated costs. Another tool, Optima HIV, is designed for epidemic projection, prioritization of HIV responses, and evaluation. It integrates a mathematical model of HIV transmission and disease progression with an economic and financial analysis framework and a formal optimization routine. This tool determines the most effective approach to achieve defined objectives, such as national strategic plan targets, while considering political, ethical, and logistical constraints. The common goal is to minimize new HIV infections and AIDS-related deaths. Optima HIV is freely available online. The World Health Organization (WHO) and collaborating organizations have developed various tools to assist with drug quantification and supply management. These tools are available for download and include descriptions of their main purposes and programmatic focus. A flexible tool has also been developed for costing investments in critical enablers, such as integrated treatment and rights literacy programs, legal services, stigma and discrimination reduction programs, and training for healthcare workers and law enforcement. Many other models and tools exist, each using different inputs to explore questions of priority for health policymakers. These tools can be applied jointly through model comparison exercises. Incorporating data from models, surveys, and special studies into regular data reviews is crucial for triangulating and validating assessments of program performance and contextualizing the data. A systems approach to improving data quality includes establishing a data quality review (DQR) process. This process helps countries ensure that their data accurately reflect the status of the populations served and the performance of their programs. A harmonized, health sector-wide framework for DQR has been developed by WHO, the Global Fund, and Gavi. This framework is applicable from the level of health facilities to the national level and complements existing systems for routine monitoring, supervision, and program evaluation. The DQR framework focuses on the quality of selected core tracer indicators across dimensions such as maternal health, immunization, HIV, and tuberculosis. It examines issues related to data completeness, accuracy, and external consistency. Countries can adapt the framework to include additional indicators based on their needs and resources. The analysis considers both program-specific and systemic issues, quantifying problems related to data completeness, accuracy, and external consistency. Data quality dimensions in the DQR include: Completeness and timeliness: Ensuring data are available and reported on time for the complete calculation of indicators. Internal consistency: Assessing the plausibility of reported data compared to historical values or expected relationships between indicators. This includes comparing reported data with source documents in health facilities. External consistency: Evaluating the agreement between two data sources measuring the same health indicator. External comparisons of population data: Assessing the adequacy of population data used in calculating health indicator denominators, such as rates or proportions. Front-end measures, such as designing data collection forms and tools, can improve data quality and reduce the time healthcare professionals spend on reporting tasks. Periodic reviews of these tools ensure alignment with current guidelines, indicator definitions, and patient flow. Analyzing data from these tools and generating outputs that help managers and stakeholders identify problems and areas for focus is a key aspect of routine data review and decision-making. A simplified and standardized methodology for these reviews is essential. This guideline supports managers in regularly reviewing data from across the HIV services cascade, supplemented periodically with data from models, surveys, and special studies to triangulate and validate program performance assessments, including impact. Routine data reviews should prioritize a simple set of selected indicators based on recommended minimum datasets, analyzed at national, subnational, and facility levels. National program managers should conduct these reviews at least annually, ideally more frequently, with a focus on geographic divisions and disaggregated data by age, gender, and key populations to highlight differences in service access and quality. Subnational area managers (e.g., provincial or district levels) may conduct more frequent data reviews, such as quarterly, while facility managers may review their data even more often to monitor progress and support staff in delivering services more efficiently and effectively. In addition to routine program data, regular evaluations and operational research systems are needed to learn from implementation, address complex questions, or test new approaches in service delivery. Evaluation, operational research, and implementation science employ research methods to complement routine data review as part of a data-driven approach to continuous quality improvement and service coverage. Given limited resources, it is crucial to focus investments on programs and services that are appropriate to needs, well-implemented, effective, and efficient. By establishing and updating a regular evaluation agenda, countries can remain focused on primary program priorities and address the most significant bottlenecks in implementation. Research and evaluation studies should be planned and managed as discrete projects with formal processes and oversight. The evaluation and research agenda should also consider feasibility, focusing on checking information and filling gaps rather than gathering redundant data. Sound design and management of evaluation and operational research require technical expertise to tailor the approach to the specific country and program context. Individual-level data are generally better suited to addressing salient research questions than aggregate data.
